title: The Hypertrophy Iceberg Explained (a complete guide to muscle growth)
summary: NH walks through roughly 150 programming and muscle-growth terms arranged as an iceberg (sky, tip, surface, depths, abyss), ordered by when each becomes relevant to a lifter's progression rather than by importance. He gives a short definition and his stance on each, stressing programming as everything for naturals, compounds, steady progression, muscular rather than mechanical failure, tonnage, top/hard sets, and dismissing pump-chasing, supplements, junk-volume fears and abyss-level minutiae.
claims: Programming is everything for natural lifters; to progress you will have to learn to program at some point
Terms like RPE, deloads, hypertrophy blocks and mesocycles come from powerlifting and are often misused in bodybuilding; he excludes them as not optimal for muscle growth
Lifting weights, with bodyweight or free weights, is superior to other forms of resistance training for growing muscle
Resistance training's one goal is to damage muscle fibers so they repair bigger
Motivation gets you into the gym but will not keep you going; later you need discipline
Warm-ups are essential; jumping straight into heavy weights will get you injured
Beginners only need to manage calories, not macros; he ignored macros for his first five years and progressed fine
For beginners any frequency works, even once or twice a week; pick what fits your schedule
Beginners must focus on technique, not weight; if technique regresses as weight rises you are on a dangerous path
Compounds put the most muscle on your frame; do not run a program of only machines and isolation, nor only heavy low-rep compounds
Soreness is not a good indicator of growth; with appropriate frequency it disappears, and he has not been sore in two years while still progressing
Progressive overload can be applied by adding weight, reps, sets, frequency or reducing rest
Novices do not need to be scientific geniuses to put on muscle
Calisthenics are ideal for weak beginners or those without a gym: push-ups, sit-ups, assisted pull-ups
Shoulder pain is usually the first pain novices get from too much benching with poor form; shoulders take forever to heal
Home training is fine for beginners and is the future of training
Novice syndrome: progressing too fast leads to burnout and quitting; being mildly intense for a year beats being super intense for six months
The real limiting factor in muscle growth is your brain, i.e. knowledge, not your body
Going to failure is very important for muscle growth; know the difference between muscle failure and lungs or heart giving out
You need a clear goal (strength, aesthetics, calisthenics, sport) to give your training direction
Switching to 5 lb plates is a hit to the ego but necessary to keep progressing
Mechanical failure (form breaking down) should be fixed by reinforcing weak areas and focusing on technique
Strength on a lift fades and the pattern is forgotten if trained less often; keep squat patterns in your training at all times to maintain neurological adaptation
Full range of motion all the time is a mistake; all ranges matter, though not equally
Do not train the big barbell lifts all the time; for progress and longevity you need other movements and respect for recovery
Isolation work is as important as compounds but hits smaller muscles; keep a balance
Stuffing your face to get stronger builds leverage via fat mass, not muscle; you will regret it
The goal is steady progression with no plateaus or breaks, not progressing like a shooting star
Supplements are useless at this stage; programming is 100 times more important
Ignore strength standards unless competing; what matters is a weight relevant to your leverages that takes you near failure
Orthodox, conventional training works; do not reinvent the wheel unless a movement causes pain
The pump is a pleasurable byproduct, not the goal; never pick reps or weights to chase a pump
Cardio is not necessary and does not kill gains, but 30 minutes of lifting beats 30 minutes of cardio
Recovery, including sleep and nutrition, is where growth is actualized; skinny people especially cannot underestimate it
Supersets save a lot of time and are not reserved for advanced lifters
Static rep schemes like 5x5, 3x5 or 10x10 are fine for beginners but do not get stuck on them
Specificity training lets you maintain neurological adaptation without repeating the same lift: choose lifts in a line of specificity with the main lift for carryover
A lifting program is unavoidable because it lets you track progress and therefore program
Animal products are good calorie and micronutrient sources but do not overdo them; a beginner eating 12 eggs is ridiculous
Lower back pain comes from squatting or deadlifting improperly or too often; it should not be a daily occurrence
Program hopping develops training ADHD and stalls you more the further you advance
Upper body bros develop imbalances; even with an upper focus, three sets of squats and three of deadlifts a week will not kill you
Top sets are the highest-quality intensity; warm-ups should lead to them and they drive progression more than they build muscle directly
Plateaus are fully avoidable with smart programming: go around the wall rather than ramming it
Track your lifts and reps even if you do not track food
Untracked finishers at the end of a session are fine; they build work capacity and do not hurt recovery
Exercise selection dictates how your physique turns out, so it is paramount
Muscle is gained mostly via weighted stretch; a negative is weighted stretch
Weak cardiovascular endurance can limit work capacity when lungs and heart give out before muscle
Micronutrients are underrated; do not eat only for macros
Constant cutting for summer is yo-yo dieting that limits progression; cut sparingly
Overfocusing on performance on one day can limit progression over the week
Volume and intensity are facets of the same thing; think of volume as reps and sets and intensity as the weight on them
Evolving rep ranges help progression; a mix of static and evolving ranges works
Steroids are never a good solution; you can get big without them
Pyramiding down risks losing top sets; be careful with that practice
Muscular failure is the goal, not mechanical failure; find ways to let the muscle fail and not the structure
Exercise variations maintain neurological adaptation, add diversity and prevent overuse injuries
Partials can be introduced deliberately to help progression on full-range lifts
Percentages of an estimated 1RM are easy to use and he recommends them over RPE for bodybuilding
Time under tension is overrated; do not slow negatives on purpose, do the best negative into the best positive
Do not use AMRAP for top sets: it lets the weight dictate the rep range; use it for finishers
Mental stamina will limit you in the long run; train mind as well as body
Seeing the template or skeleton behind a program shows your programming knowledge is progressing
95-98% of injuries occur during the negative or its reversal, so a controlled negative is injury prevention
Most people do better on an omnivorous diet than vegan, carnivore or keto
Knee pain comes from squatting too often with poor form; program as many hip hinges as knee flexions
Body fat percentage becomes relevant when you start shaping aesthetics; choose leaner or fluffier by preference
Intermediate syndrome is staying intermediate for life due to lack of programming knowledge
Small muscles can be hit more often but not as hard: they burn out quickly in a session yet recover fast; big muscles are the opposite
A hard set is a type of top set and the toughest set of the day; the whole session is built around it
Form is not absolute and must be adapted to the individual, but beginners need rigid rules first, like kids need structure
Weekly and daily set counts matter, and you should understand reps before sets
Nucleus overload adds easy, low-fatigue sets to accumulate volume for lagging body parts
Priming the CNS: order lifts so earlier ones warm you up for later ones, avoiding repeated warm-ups
Dirty bulking in the depths just makes you fat and harms your health
The baseline is dug into as you train; when continuing no longer makes sense the session should end
Rest-pause and positive-only work waste top sets and negatives for non-advanced lifters
Mind-muscle connection does not grow muscle by magic; its value is in finding the technique that recruits the muscle
Pre-fatigue only makes sense for advanced lifters; earlier it masks poor technique
Giant sets require strong cardio; done too early they compromise failure and progression
Staying about 25% above minimum recoverable volume without exceeding the maximum is fine; it is not a razor-thin line
Tonnage (volume times intensity, distributed by frequency) is the key: strength matters for bodybuilding only to progress relevant tonnage
In advanced stages progression must be schemed deliberately rather than happening by default
Junk volume is overblown; volume is only junk when it replaces hard sets, e.g. a set of 25 instead of a hard set of 5-6
SARMs, like steroids, should be avoided
Tendinitis cannot be fixed by rest alone; train around it to rehab
Recomposition is the most advanced and most suitable diet for patient long-term lifters unless you have an extreme body type
Hormones are most likely fine; no need for TRT, only advanced lifters should think about hormone strategies
Eat your vegetables; plants should make up a big portion of your diet
Training must be sustainable over years, not intense for six weeks then burnt out
Rotations swap lifts in the same line of specificity on given days, a form of autoregulation unnecessary for beginners
SI joint pain can only be fixed by programming lower body days and recovery properly
Intensity windows define the weight, reps and sets that produce progression; outside them nothing happens
The red zone is the bottom of the negative into the positive where most injuries occur; master it and you will rarely get hurt
Back-off sets follow hard sets and are a safe way to accumulate volume
Blood flow restriction is pointless and potentially dangerous for novices
Bands and chains are unnecessary for hypertrophy
Negatives-only training is impractical and of little relevance
He spent about three years in the sky, three on the tip and two at the surface before reaching the depths
Artificial failure (pump, blood occlusion) is not true muscular failure
Compound lifts deliver diffuse tonnage spread across many muscles; advanced lifters should think about the distribution
Relative intensity: 80% at the end of a workout is not 80% at the start, so programming only with absolute intensity misprograms
Biomechanics are oversold to beginners; lift with good form and what feels good
Sandbagging is not bad when used to prepare for maximal days; many people sandbag too much when deloading
He likes reps in reserve for longevity and injury prevention despite the tonnage sacrifice
He has his perfect program, flexible enough that he never needs to change it
Spinal decompression matters for anyone squatting and deadlifting a lot
Metabolic stress accounts for maybe 3-4% of progression and is not worth focusing on

keep squat patterns in every program
